**RESEARCH**
# **Forecasting the software engineering model’s effort estimation using** **constructive cost estimation models**

**Mohammed Naif Alatawi** **[1]**

Received: 24 January 2024 / Accepted: 24 May 2024 / Published online: 13 June 2024
© The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2024

**Abstract**

Machine learning models are increasingly being developed to solve various problems in academic and corporate settings.
However, data scientists encounter multiple challenges during model development that require software engineering methodologies to overcome. In many cases, developers working on machine learning projects may need to fully realize the benefits
of adhering to the steps outlined in the Software Engineering Development Lifecycle. It is essential to recognize that the
development processes for machine learning systems differ from those of traditional software systems. Therefore, it is crucial
to investigate how software engineering principles can be adapted or applied to the machine learning workflow. This paper
explores such practices and problems from a software engineering perspective. To achieve this, we utilized the COCOMO
II Model to predict a software engineering model’s effort estimation and effort estimation incorporating machine learning
hybrid techniques. Specifically, we employed a Genetic Algorithm-based Support Vector Regressor, which yielded the highest
PRED value for effort estimation using the COCOMO II Model. Overall, this study provides insights into the application of
software engineering methodologies for building machine learning models and highlights the importance of incorporating
these practices to optimize the development process and achieve more accurate effort estimation.

**Keywords** Machine learning · Software engineering · Artificial neural network


**1 Introduction**

Software development projects often face challenges in accurately estimating the time and effort required for completion.
The primary responsibility of software engineering is effort
estimation based on analogies. The effort required for new
software projects was calculated for the corresponding development and management using the existing histories [1].
Over the years, various models and methodologies have
been developed to address this issue, with the COCOMO
(Constructive Cost Model) being one of the most prominent. COCOMO has undergone several iterations to adapt to
the evolving landscape of software development practices.
Constructive Cost Model is widely used for software project
cost prediction because it improves capital accuracy [2–4].

B Mohammed Naif Alatawi

alatawimn@ut.edu.sa

1 Information Technology Department, Faculty of Computers
and Information Technology, University of Tabuk, Tabuk
City, Saudi Arabia


COCOMO I, also known as COCOMO’81, provided a foundational framework for estimating software development
costs, primarily based on the waterfall lifecycle. However,
the need for a more comprehensive estimation model became
apparent as software development methodologies evolved
to include rapid development processes, reuse-driven techniques, and object-oriented approaches. This led to the
development of COCOMO II, which incorporates modern
lifecycle processes and capabilities. COCOMO II introduces
three distinct models: the Application Composition Model,
the Early Design Model, and the Post-Architecture Model.
These models cater to different stages of the software development lifecycle, addressing prototyping, system layout,
and code creation, respectively. One of the most critical
tasks in software development is software development effort
estimation or SDEE. The success of software projects is significantly impacted by accurate work estimation in the early
stages of the software design life cycle.
The parameters of the parametric, data-driven SDEE
model COCOMO (Constructive Cost Model) must be
adjusted using local data from the organization to provide an
appropriate estimate [5–7]. By considering factors such as
## 123

736 Iran Journal of Computer Science (2024) 7:735–754


software reuse, reengineering, and various effort multipliers,
COCOMO II aims to provide more accurate and versatile
cost estimation. This paper focuses on the COCOMO II
Post-Architecture Model and its application in estimating
software development efforts. We delve into the dataset used
for validation, NASA 93, which includes effort multipliers
and other parameters crucial for COCOMO II calculations.
Additionally,weexploreusingmeta-heuristictechniqueslike
genetic algorithms (GA) for feature selection and support
vector regression (SVR) for refining effort estimation. Our
analysis highlights the effectiveness of integrating machine
learning approaches with established software engineering
models like COCOMO II. By leveraging the strengths of
both disciplines, we strive to enhance the accuracy and reliability of software development effort estimation, ultimately
contributing to more successful project planning and man
agement.
The digital revolution makes possible data- or modeldriven digital goods and services. This paves the way for
cutting-edge technologies like machine translation, driverless cars, and preventative maintenance [8]. Data-driven
software components are fundamental to these kinds of
products. An example of a data-driven software component performs a specific task (such as image segmentation,
sentiment analysis, classification, etc.) using data science
techniques. Data-driven software components have some or
all of their functionality derived (learned) from data rather
than defined (coded) by the programmer in the traditional
sense [9, 10].
The model concept is essential to every software module
that relies on data (or several models coupled in a pipeline).
The software component’s input and output relationship
is typically nonlinear, marking a fundamental difference
in behaviour from conventional (i.e., not data-driven) software. Because of this, even a seemingly insignificant change
in the inputs can result in significant output differences.
Uncertainty in results for unseen data arises because this
input–output relationship is defined only for some of the data
(or when the modelled system changes, i.e. if there is concept
drift). Various algorithms exist for accomplishing any given
goal (for example, neural networks, support vector machines,
and decision trees can all solve classification tasks) [11, 12].
Understanding the behaviour of a data-driven software
component requires more than just familiarity with the algorithm(s) used to develop it. Before anything else, the training
and inference data must be taken into account (i.e., runtime)

[13, 14]. As a second point, standard software engineering
development principles like encapsulation and modularity
must be re-examined. To retrain a data-driven component, for
instance, one must alter its application context (its intended
scope), the sort of model employed, or the internal parame
ters.
## 123


Standards establish necessary effort estimation properties of a software system and its components to assure the
intended effort estimation of the system. ISO/IEC 25010
(ISO/IEC, 2011) is one standard that provides effort estimation models for software and systems, i.e. a hierarchy
of effort estimation features of interest and how to quantify
and assess them. Due to their unique characteristics, these
effort estimation models cannot be used directly, as with
data-driven software components. Several require revisions
to their definition (such as the reusability of trained models),
and others should be added (e.g., trustworthiness, fairness).
We also need to be specific about which characteristics are
essential for certain features of the whole system. The methods used to run a model are often secondary in importance
to other factors in data-driven software systems, such as the
type of model or the data utilized for training and testing.
One must be familiar with the use case’s application context and the specific data-driven approach to create helpful
effortestimationmodels.Inthispost,weprovideasystematic
approach to building effort estimation models for Machine
Learning (ML) systems, using a real-world application as our
inspiration.
The problem addressed in this research revolves around
the challenge of accurately estimating the effort required for
software development projects. The hypothesis proposed to
tackle this problem is that integrating a hybrid algorithm
combining Support Vector Regression (SVR) and Genetic
Algorithm (GA) can enhance the accuracy and reliability of
effort estimation models in software engineering. By leveraging the complementary strengths of SVR and GA, the hybrid
algorithm aims to optimize feature selection and parameter tuning, thereby improving the predictive performance of
effort estimation models. This hypothesis forms the basis of
our proposed solution, which has been explored and validated through empirical experimentation and analysis in this

research.

The paper’s significant contribution is in investigating
the application of software engineering methodologies to
developing machine learning models. Specifically, the paper
explores the challenges and best practices for building
machine learning models from a software engineering perspective, focusing on improving the development process’s
efficiency and accuracy. To achieve this, the paper applies
the COCOMO II Model to predict a software engineering
model’s effort estimation and effort estimation that incorporates machine learning hybrid techniques. The paper uses
a Genetic Algorithm-based Support Vector Regressor to
estimate the effort required for building machine-learning
models. This approach allows developers to assess better the
time and resources necessary for building machine learning
models, which can improve project planning and management. The paper aims to provide insights into integrating
software engineering methodologies and machine learning

Iran Journal of Computer Science (2024) 7:735–754 737


workflows, enabling developers to build more reliable, scalable, and maintainable models. This can help overcome
challenges associated with developing machine learning
models, such as data quality, model selection, and hyperparameter tuning, and make the development process more
efficient and effective.
The contributions of this paper can be outlined as follows:

- Development of a Novel Hybrid Algorithm:
We introduce a novel hybrid algorithm combining Support
Vector Regression (SVR) and Genetic Algorithm (GA) to
estimate software effort. This hybrid approach capitalizes
on the strengths of both techniques to improve the accuracy
and reliability of effort estimation models.

- Integration of Feature Selection and Parameter Optimiza
tion:

Our algorithm integrates feature selection and parameter
optimizationwithinasingleframework.ByemployingGA
for feature selection, we identify the most relevant features
for effort estimation while simultaneously optimizing the
parameters of the SVR model to enhance predictive per
formance.

- Comprehensive Evaluation Framework:
We establish a comprehensive evaluation framework for
assessing the proposed algorithm’s performance. This
framework includes various performance metrics, such
as Mean Magnitude of Relative Error (MMRE) and
Predicted Value (PRED), thoroughly analyzing the algorithm’s effectiveness and reliability.

- Comparison with Existing Approaches:
We compare our algorithm with existing approaches to
software effort estimation. By benchmarking against stateof-the-art methods, we demonstrate our hybrid algorithm’s
superior accuracy and robustness.

- Insights into Software Engineering Practices:
Through our research, we provide insights into applying
machine learning techniques in software engineering practices. By bridging the gap between machine learning and
software engineering, our algorithm offers valuable contributions to advancing both fields.

Overall, this paper’s contributions lie in developing an
innovative hybrid algorithm, integrating feature selection
and parameter optimization, establishing a comprehensive
evaluation framework, conducting comparative analyses
with existing approaches, and providing insights into software engineering practices. These contributions collectively
advance the state-of-the-art in software effort estimation and

pave the way for future research in the field.
Furthermore, this research is divided into five sections.
Section 1 introduces the current research with problem
formulation and objectives. Section 2 shows the literature
related to the current study. Section 3 shows the current


research methodology. Section 4 shows the results of current
research with discussion and limitations, while Sect. 5 shows

the conclusions of this research with recommendations and

future work.

**2 Related work**

The development of machine learning models has become
increasingly important in both academic and industrial settings, as they are used to solve a wide variety of problems,
such as predictive maintenance, image recognition, natural
language processing, and recommendation systems, to name
a few. However, building effective and efficient machine
learningmodelsisacomplextaskthatinvolvesseveralstages,
such as data collection, pre-processing, feature engineering,
model selection, training, and evaluation [9, 10]. Each stage
presents challenges and requires machine learning and software engineering expertise. While software engineering has
well-established methodologies for developing traditional
softwaresystems,suchastheSoftwareEngineeringDevelopmentLifecycle,thesemethodologiesdonotnecessarilyapply
to developing machine learning models. Machine learning
models involve software development, statistical modelling,
and data processing [15, 16].
Moreover, machine learning models often require a lot
of experimentation, as different algorithms and hyperparameters may need to be tried before finding the optimal
solution. Therefore, there is a need to investigate the challenges and best practices for building machine learning
modelsfromasoftwareengineeringperspective.Byapplying
software engineering methodologies to the machine learning
workflow, developers can ensure that their models are reliable, maintainable, and scalable while also improving the
efficiency of the development process. This is particularly
important as machine learning models become more pervasive and critical to business operations [11, 17, 18].
For decades, experts in Software Engineering (SE) have
been refining techniques, processes, and tools for designing, maintaining, and putting together sophisticated pieces
of software. By definition, software engineering is the study
of engineering applied to the design, development, and
maintenance of software, with the primary goal of improving software development processes and techniques, such
as making it easier to adapt to larger systems and more
cost-effective to produce high-effort estimation software.
Surpassing even its own lofty goals, SE has led to significant developments in its practices and procedures. In light of
these developments, it is crucial to comprehend how software
developers could modify their current procedures to incorporate or modify the existing SE process into their Machine
Learning (ML) workflows. From a software engineering vantage point, we explore the issues and solutions that crop up
## 123

738 Iran Journal of Computer Science (2024) 7:735–754


during the creation of ML models. Since it could be argued
thatdatascientistswouldbenefitfromadoptingclassicalsoftware engineering disciplines (such as systems design, effort
estimation assurance, and verification) to build their models
properly, we centre our analysis on the well-known stages
presented in the Software Engineering development process
and investigate how software developers could benefit from
applying or adapting these processes to the ML workflow

[10, 19, 20].
The primary purpose of this research [21] is to do an
all-encompassing evaluation of ML models concerning four
criteria: ML technique, estimation accuracy, model comparison, and estimation setup. An extensive literature analysis
was conducted, during which the empirical studies on ML
models published during the past two decades were analyzed (1991–2010). In total, 84 primary studies were used
to compile this meta-analysis. From this literature review,
the Author learned that eight different ML techniques were
utilized for SDEE models. Regarding estimation, these ML
models are virtually as accurate as non-ML models. As a
bonus, different ML models are ideally suited for application in different estimation scenarios due to their unique
benefits and drawbacks. The application of ML models to
SDEE could be pretty fruitful. Even while ML models have
gained much traction recently, they still need more publicity
and incentives to be widely used in businesses. Based on the
findings of this review, the Author provides suggestions for
future research and tips for practitioners.
The authors of the study [22] conducted a systematic
review of prior research in the field and five qualitative interviews with software developers who use or want to use AI
tools in their daily work to evaluate the current state of development, the potential for future development, and the risks
of AI application to software engineering. Lessons learned
throughout the software development life cycle are categorized in this study. Three areas were identified as particularly
fruitful and promising for AI development: the systematic
evaluation of these data in neural networks, the structured
analysis of big data pools to discover patterns and novel information clusters and the automation of lengthy routine jobs
in software development and testing using algorithms, such
as for debugging and documentation. The development process can be accelerated, costs can be reduced, and efficiency
gains can be realized with the help of artificial intelligence.
Automating software engineering activities has a significant
advantage. When humans use AI tools properly, they can
unleash an exponential increase in creative output, whereas
traditional AI has relied on artificial structures and has primarily been reproductive.
Uncertainty is introduced into a system when learning
is incorporated into it. Authors wondered how the growing interest in embedding machine learning into systems
might alter how programs are constructed. The Author used
## 123


qualitative and quantitative methods, including 14 in-depth
interviews and 342 survey responses from 26 countries spanning four continents, to identify critical differences between
the evolution of machine learning and non-machine learning systems. This study [23] reveals differences in software
engineering (including requirements, design, testing, and
process) and workplace characteristics. As a result of this
investigation, the Author proposes further lines of inquiry
and practical applications.
An exploratory multivariate data visualization tool
allowed us to analyze the results of various aggregation
techniques and the role of aggregation in understanding
multivariate data. Finally, the Author applied this method
to Multi-criteria Ranking to ensure its generalizability. The
Author tested it by analyzing and ranking potential solutions
to a decision-making scenario drawn from the real world.
Furthermore, this approach [24] was applied to the study
of machine learning. The author evaluated the consistency
and faithfulness of the original variables of the aggregated
results against a set of test cases that included regression. The
results confirmed this approach’s efficacy, accuracy, sensitivity, outlier detection capability, scalability, and multi-criteria
decision-making support. When no ground truth is available,
this method can act as a neutral unsupervised predictor, and
it can be used in other areas where aggregating data in hierarchically structured models is required.
Artificial intelligence (AI) methods to resolve issues in
software development have recently seen a rise in interest. This body of work represents both new developments
in search-based software engineering and more traditional
studies in probabilistic reasoning and machine learning in
software engineering. This study [25] delves deeply into the
binds holding these two disciplines together, stating that they
have a lot in common and highlighting some future hurdles
that must be cleared before AI can be utilized correctly in
software engineering.
This goal necessitated a reorientation of an organization’s
development practices. The Author reports on this study [26]
of Microsoft’s software engineers as they create AI-powered
apps. The Author considers a nine-step workflow approach
based on this experience developing artificial intelligence
(AI) applications (such as search and natural language processing) and data science tools (application diagnostics and
bug reporting). To shed light on several critical engineering difficulties that businesses may face when developing
enterprise-level AI solutions, the Author discovered that several Microsoft teams have unified this process into existing,
highly developed, Agile-like software engineering procedures. The Author gathered answers from a few Microsoft
teams about these issues. Authors have also identified three
characteristics of AI that set it apart from other software
application fields: AI components are more difficult to handle as distinct modules than traditional software components;

Iran Journal of Computer Science (2024) 7:735–754 739


models may be ‘entangled’ in complex ways and experience
non-monotonic error behaviour and customizing and reusing
models call for skills rarely found in software teams. The
Author believes that other businesses can profit from learning from Microsoft’s teams’ experiences.
The dissemination of research [27] findings mostly
depends on textual communication. However, this advancement can be slowed down by the absence of reviewers to ensure the effort estimation of published research
papers. Refereeing in such a context must rely on automated approaches to check individual words and phrases
in submissions for recurring rhetorical devices. This study
aims to compare and contrast different supervised machinelearning techniques used to perform genre analysis in the first
paragraphs of articles about software engineering. A semisupervised approach was adopted to increase the number of
annotated sentences. A support vector machine and a logistic
regression were used to calculate an F-score for genre analysis in the corpus. Using a method built on logistic regression
and BERT, the authors successfully retrieved patterns in a
genre analysis, yielding an F-score of 88.25.
In a study [28], the authors examine the major problems
when software engineers use machine learning techniques.
To identify these challenges, the Author conducted a Systematic Review across eight different search engines to identify
papers describing the difficulties researchers faced when
attempting to implement machine learning methods and tools
tocarryoutsoftwareengineeringprojects.Thus,thisresearch
aims to classify and discuss eight challenges: data labelling,
data inconsistency, data costs, data complexity, data scarcity,
inapplicability of results, model parameterization, and model
effort estimation. This research can help those interested in
implementing ML into software engineering projects anticipate the most common difficulties they will face.
In recent years, numerous studies [29] have found success using machine learning methods. As a result, many
different deep learning models exist, each fine-tuned for a
specific software goal. There are many advantages of using
deep learning models in software engineering. Up-to-date
software testing and upkeep have never been more critical.

The primary goal of this research [30] was to identify
the difficulties in developing ML software and to propose a

difficulties. Although there is much potential in machine


learning (ML), only approximately 20% of ML software

the provided solutions will help advance the research agenda.

machine learning for software project risk management [31].
There is a display with the ratings separated into two categories. Project management-related surveys and research

more efficient in reducing the project’s fault, which is essential for further decreasing the probability chances effectively
and increasing the software development performance ratio.
AccordingtostudiesconductedbyShepperdetal.[32],the
team’s expertise in developing a defect prediction model substantially impacts the model’s final performance. This study
critically analyses Shepperd et al.’s findings from a different
angle. The significant correlation between the research group
effect and other parameters makes isolating the impact of a
research group on a model’s performance difficult. Considering this strong association, the Author discovered that the
family of measures is more influential than the research team.
From these findings, the Author concludes that researchers’
propensity to recycle experimental components accounts for
the observed relationship between the research group and
defect prediction model performance. Scientists can better
eliminate bias and generate reliable findings using various

data sources and metrics.

**3 Materials and methods**

This section explains the methodology of current research.
Estimating a software project’s cost is crucial in any software management plan. Accurate cost estimating is vital
because it allows for the proper categorization and prioritization of development initiatives, facilitating resource
allocation and optimizing utilization. Management effectivenessisdependentontheprecisionofthesoftwareengineering
specifications. Estimation of work, time to create, cost, team
size, risk assessment, etc., are all examples of such variables.
These forecasts are often made during the earliest stages
of a project’s development. Therefore, a reliable model is
required to determine these values. Having fewer disagreements later in the project’s development is possible with an
early and accurate estimation methodology.
Based on the COCOMO model, this work proposes a GASVR method to estimate software costs using the perceptron
learning algorithm. Research has shown that GA-SVR is one
of the most effective methods for evaluating software prices.
Many experts in the field are currently focusing their attention on improving GA-SVR-based software cost estimation

methods.

**3.1 Software cost estimation**

To provide a rough estimate of the amount of time and
money that will be required to finish a software engineering
project, the purpose of software cost estimates is to provide that estimate. Estimating software expenses may appear
straightforward in theory, but doing it in practice brings several problems and complications that must be overcome. The
vast majority of methods for estimating the cost of software
development emphasize the human component, and they provide estimates in terms of person-months worked. It does
so by computing the time and effort required to complete a
software project, considering various criteria such as deadlines, the acquisition of resources, and the limits imposed
by cost. Accurate estimates are needed to design software
successfully and efficiently. Experts in the software business
have created various strategies for cost estimation over several decades. Yet, the primary challenge faced by those in
software engineering has remained the same. Early software


estimating models were founded on the principles of regression analysis and mathematical derivations. The COCOMO
II model is the one that sees the most excellent use among
these several approaches. Examples of modern modelling
techniquesincludesimulation,neuralnetworks,geneticalgorithms, soft computing, and fuzzy logic modelling, to name
just a few. In this study, we optimize the existing coefficients
that calculate the best estimate of the future effort required to
develop software utilizing the COCOMO II model by applying the most prevalent genetic algorithm in conjunction with
the support vector machine method. This method was chosen because it has become increasingly popular in recent
years. In evolutionary computing, genetic algorithms are a
type of algorithm for optimizing populations. They were initially invented in 1975 by a scientist from the Netherlands.
It is a heuristic algorithm that is derived from nature, and
it has the capability of producing approximative as well as
precise outcomes when it is put to use. To incrementally
improve upon the previously obtained best answer, this algorithm works with a solution set rather than a single solution.

**3.2 Genetic algorithm**

The genetic method (GA) is a search algorithm that randomly
explores solutions for the best one. Like biological genes,
they act similarly. Once the examination is complete, it will
be restored to mint condition. Gene expression analysis (GA)
displays genes about chromosomal status. The chromosomes
should be free to exchange, mutate, and self-select. These
answers are improved after the competition because of the
selection process. All of the chromosomes are generated at
random. The objective function determines the fitness value
it receives. The chromosome will recombine, change, and
be selected by its fitness. In a crossover, two parents (sets
of chromosomes) are chosen randomly, and their genes are
swapped. Then, a new set of chromosomes, a “child,” will
be produced. To mutate is to alter one or more chromosomes
arbitrarily. More chromosomes can be generated via crossing and mutation, and their relative fitness can be determined.
Then, we randomly choose from among them using a roulette
wheel. The chosen chromosomes will be used in the subse
quent assessment.
Soft computing techniques such as neural networks,
genetic algorithms, fuzzy logic modelling, and others are
the foundation of today’s software development effort estimation models. These models are used to find the most
accurate and precise predictions regarding software development time and effort. The neural networks and fuzzy
approaches are challenging to apply due to the absence of
any definitive guidelines for their creation. The genetic algorithm can potentially be a valid extra tool for software effort
estimation, and it can significantly improve accuracy. This
technique is known as a nonparametric one since it does
## 123

742 Iran Journal of Computer Science (2024) 7:735–754

**Fig. 1** Support vector regression


not presuppose anything about how the data are organized.
Instead, it develops equations based solely on the values fitted to the data. A genetic algorithm is an evolved strategy
to estimate the required work. The solution is obtained by
employing a cycle of generations of candidate solutions;

each whittled down based on the criterion of “survival of

the fittest.” Genetic Programming, sometimes known as GP,
is a method of global search that reduces the likelihood of
being mired in the local optimal solution. This method is
unique compared to others, such as neural networks and gradient descent, which are susceptible to forming local optimal
values. It is beneficial for challenging tasks, mainly when
minimal information is available about the underlying search
space and the concept is simple to grasp.

**3.3 Support vector regressor**

Vapnik introduced the support vector machine, which is
based on the notion of minimizing structural risk and the
Chervonenkis dimension.

Let’s pretend we have the following data set: *(xi*, *yi)...*
*(Xi*, *yi)*, *xi Rn*, *yi R*, *i* � 1, 2, 3 *...l* . Knowing that *y* �
*f* ( *x* ) in *R* space, we can zero in on the target function *f* ( *x* ) in
*Rn* space. *yi* �−1or1 Indicates a categorization difficulty.
Figure 1 depicts the case where it is an actual number, as in
a regression problem.
It is assumed that there is little difference between *f* ( *x* )
and *yi* when *f* ( *x* ) � *w* ∗ *x* + *b* .
In that case, we can provide the most accurate prediction
possible. And the best plane that can be found using SVR is

*w* .

demonstrated in Fig. 2, exceptional cases always complicate

**3.4.1 Chromosomes**

The chromosome was placed in a *Q* - array. The number of
chromosomes, or *Q*, and the number of bits, or *a*, in a single
chromosome, respectively. We have x chromosomes and y
bits in each chromosome if we have n unknowns to solve.

When this is the case, we may use Fig. 3 to determine that
our array size is between [ *x*, *n* ∗ *y* ].

Iran Journal of Computer Science (2024) 7:735–754 743


**Fig. 3** Array of chromosomes

**3.4.2 Crossover**

In this scenario, we only use a single crossover point. Let’s
randomly choose two chromosomes and set their length to 1.
In a normal distribution, the crossover point is between − 1
and 1. Two new chromosomes are produced when we switch

what’s on either side of the crossover site.

**3.4.3 Mutation**

The analysis in this paper uses a point mutation. We will
randomly select some DNA from a chromosome, changing
a 0 in a bit to a 1 if it is present. If the bit value is 1, then
change it to 0. Systems employing mechanisms conceptually
comparable to a roulette wheel are utilized.

**3.4.4 Features selection**

Every chromosome can be assigned a fit value by applying
the fit function. This is fantastic news if the fit value is significant. Because it requires less space on the steering wheel.
Additionally, we utilize probabilistic logic to pick the chro
mosomal.

**3.4.5 GA-SVR**

GASVR accepts the following flags in its command line output: -s (SVR type), -t (kernel type), -c (cost), -g (gamma), and
-p (precision) (epsilon). We use epsilon-SVR with a radial

basis function kernel for the SVR.

In this study, the three variables employed to solve the
problem are metaphorically represented as chromosomes.


Crossover, mutation, and natural selection are then applied to
the chromosome. After a few generations, the best setting for
SVR’s parameters emerges. If appropriately used, SVR has
the potential to produce the most reliable prediction model
and result. The process flowchart is shown in Fig. 4.
Thus, attempts to broaden the models’ applicability typically result in mediocre performance. We need a technique
that can handle this situation without requiring human
intervention. Machine learning will always be the answer.
Nowadays, it’s easier and faster than ever to learn new information, classify data, spot trends, etc. This work explored
ways to improve software project timeline estimates by
applying Machine Learning techniques within the Software
Engineering discipline. We may employ an SVR to model
complex relationships between your dependent and independent variables. When work is considered a dependent
property and cost and software size are treated as independent
elements, SVRs become helpful machine-learning tools.
Data for the COCOMO model’s training cost parameters (size, effort, cost, time, and quality) will be obtained
from Kaggle.com and pre-trained. In this research, we built
an estimation model for COCOMO using a support vector
regression and a genetic algorithm. We are employing the
SVR model to create a software effort estimation model. The

GA’s compressed data representation is sufficient for dimensionality reduction and feature selection applications.
The GA architecture that enables reduced representation
is essential to the learning process. The best layout minimizes
the reconstruction error for these two variables (RMSE).
The buried layer’s combined weight expression needs to
be more intuitively apparent. In this example, we’ve kept
things on the bare minimum. When a node *j* was triggered,
the significance of a variable d at that node was crucial. The
greater the importance of a variable, the more significant its
weight.
This means that the importance of a variable across all J

nodes

than a predetermined threshold.

**3.5 Methodological theorem**

The evolutionary algorithm has been proposed to achieve this
optimization of the COCOMO II Post Architecture model
coefficients.Below,webreakoutthealgorithm’smostcrucial

components:

Generate individuals randomly,

*e.g.xxxx* | *xxxx* | *xxxx* | *xxxxabcd*

Four genes exist for each of the four coefficients listed
above, and their products are positive integers between zero
and nine. The first gene in a coefficient represents an integral
value, whereas the other three represent fractional values.

Iran Journal of Computer Science (2024) 7:735–754 745


Use the coefficients from a single individual i to anticipate
how much work will go into developing each Project *j* in the

dataset.

Using the following equation, we may determine whether
or not Person I is physically capable of completing Task *j* .

Fitness *i j* � [|][Actual][ −] [Estimated] *[i ]* *[j]* [|], (7)

Actual *j*

*i* —the individual number, *j* —the project number, *Actual* −
*isactualsof twareprojectef f ort Estimatedi j.*
Itistheestimatedorpredictedsoftwareprojecteffortusing

individual i.

For a project’s actual effort to be greater than its predicted
effort, the fitness value must be greater than zero, while the
opposite is valid for a negative fitness value [8].
To determine an individual’s fitness level, we take the
mean of their attained fitness levels across all Projects. The
fitness worth is proportional to the discrepancy between
actual and anticipated development effort. Because of this,
the value of the fitness function should be decreased.

*Fitnessi* � *n* [1] [∗] � *Fitnessi j*, *j* � 1 *. . . n*, (8)

*i* —the individual number, *j* —the project number, *n* —the
number of projects.
Whenever the halting condition is met, the algorithm is
finished running. Instead, a population’s optimal (minimum)
and mean fitness levels can be employed.
The selection process is a competition.

Individuals are used to create new individuals based on

the criteria chosen in an earlier step. The standard crossover
method is implemented.
In mutation, no individuals or a few individuals are chosen randomly. The odds of being chosen should be modest,
usually hovering around 10%. A unique pattern of random
gene mutations is established for each person.
Once the new population has been produced, the best individuals from both the parent and offspring populations are
selected using the same criteria. Including elitism in the plan
is one way to ensure the best possible answer is not over
looked.

The main differences between the proposed algorithm
and existing approaches lie in the methodology, optimization techniques, and performance metrics utilized. Here are
the key distinctions:
Hybridization Technique
Our proposed algorithm combines Support Vector Regression (SVR) with Genetic Algorithm (GA) in a hybrid
approach. This hybridization leverages the strengths of both
techniques, with GA used for feature selection and parameter
optimization while SVR handles the actual estimation task.


In contrast, other algorithms may rely solely on SVR or
other regression techniques without incorporating GA-based
feature selection and optimization.

Feature Selection

In our approach, GA enables efficient feature selection
by identifying the most relevant features to improve effort
estimation accuracy. GA explores the search space to identify
optimal feature subsets that contribute most significantly to
the estimation process.
Many existing algorithms may use traditional feature
selection methods or may not emphasize feature selection
as prominently as our approach does.
Optimization Parameters
Our algorithm optimizes both the features selected for
estimation and the parameters of the SVR model using GA.
This comprehensive optimization process aims to improve
the effort estimation model’s overall accuracy and robust
ness.

Other algorithms may focus solely on optimizing model
parameters or use different optimization techniques that do

not involve feature selection.

Performance Metrics

We evaluate our algorithm’s performance using metrics
such as Mean Magnitude of Relative Error (MMRE) and
Predicted Value (PRED). These metrics provide insights into
the accuracy and reliability of the effort estimation model.
While other algorithms may also use performance metrics
for evaluation, the specific metrics chosen and their interpretation may vary.
Overall, the proposed algorithm stands out due to its innovative hybridization approach, emphasis on feature selection
using GA, comprehensive optimization of model parameters,
and rigorous performance metrics evaluation. These differences contribute to our algorithm’s unique effectiveness and
performance compared to existing approaches in software

effort estimation.

**4 Results and discussions**

The datasets utilized in the research experiments include the
NASA 93 dataset, commonly used in software engineering
research for cost estimation purposes. This dataset provides
valuable information on various software projects, including
project size, effort, and other relevant metrics. The general
results of the research experiments include improvements
in the accuracy and reliability of effort estimation models
using the proposed hybrid algorithm. The hybrid algorithm,
combining Support Vector Regression (SVR) and Genetic
Algorithm (GA), demonstrated superior performance compared to traditional methods, as evidenced by reduced Mean
Absolute Error Magnitude (MMRE) and Mean Magnitude
of Relative Error (MdMRE) values.
## 123

746 Iran Journal of Computer Science (2024) 7:735–754


The equations presented in the research paper repre
sent mathematical formulations derived from established

methodologies such as COCOMO II and the proposed hybrid
algorithm. These equations are designed to capture the
relationships between various factors influencing effort estimation in software engineering. The intuition behind each
equation lies in its ability to model the complex interactions
between project attributes, algorithm parameters, and predictive accuracy. The selection of parameter values for the
algorithm is based on a combination of empirical experimentation,domainexpertise,andalgorithmicconsiderations.
Parameters are chosen to optimize the algorithm’s performance, balancing factors such as computational efficiency,
predictive accuracy, and robustness. Detailed justifications
for parameter selections are provided to ensure transparency
and reproducibility of the research findings. The study’s
main findings include developing and validating a hybrid
algorithm combining Support Vector Regression (SVR) and
Genetic Algorithm (GA) for software effort estimation. The
hybrid algorithm demonstrated improved accuracy and reliability compared to traditional methods, as evidenced by
reduced error metrics and enhanced predictive performance
across various software projects. The study’s strengths lie in
its comprehensive approach to addressing the challenge of
software effort estimation, including the development of a
novel hybrid algorithm and empirical validation using realworld datasets. However, limitations include the reliance on
specific datasets and assumptions inherent in the modelling
approach, which may affect the generalizability of the findings to different contexts.

**4.1 COCOMO model II**

Costs associated with creating software can be estimated
using the regression-based COCOMO model. In 1981, Dr.
Barry Boehm was the first to use it. This is one of the
most widely used and thoroughly explained approaches to
calculating the time and effort required to create software.
COCOMO I, also known as COCOMO’81, was an influential model back then. Software development is based on the
waterfall lifecycle [4]. Cost estimates for software developed
usingmodernlifecycleprocessesandcapabilities,suchasthe
rapid-development process model, reuse-driven techniques,
and object-oriented approaches, have been a source of contention for the company. In light of these needs, COCOMO
II, the most recent iteration, was developed. COCOMO II can
measure the size of an object in KLOC, FP, or OP. COCOMO
II takes into account software reuse and reengineering. A
large-scale, ongoing data collection and analysis project is
built on the new model to refine and calibrate its estimation
capabilities. The three separate models that make up this

whole are described in detail below:
## 123


**4.1.1 Application composition model**

The Application Composition Model uses prototyping
to address high-risk issues. Potential areas for development include interfaces, software/system interactions, performance, and technological developments. Point values
assigned to objects are used for scaling.

**4.1.2 Early design model**

Investigating various software and system layouts is a necessary part of the Early Design Model. Function points and
several other cost drivers must be considered to size the system properly.

**4.1.3 Post-architecture**

The post-architecture (PA) Model focuses on creating and
keeping working code. The size of a program can be roughly
estimated by counting the number of source instructions and
function points used in its development. This Figure is then
adjusted for factors such as software redeployment and the

likelihood of errors. Since not all COCOMO II extensions

have been calibrated, treating them all as experiments is currently safest. The calibrated program only works with the

Post Architecture model.

**4.2 Dataset description NASA 93**

COCOMO II NASA 93’s cost estimation model uses cal
endar months and 152 h (and includes development and
management hours). COCOMO predicts a nonlinear increase
in effort proportional to the size of the software (months �
*a* - KSLOC *b* - *c* ). More than a dozen "effort multipliers" are
added to arrive at c, and KSLOC is computed directly or
through function point analysis. The values for ( *a*, *b* ) are
specific to the area under investigation. To rephrase, the equation for calculating months is as follows: (KSLOC *b* ) * *a* (EM1* EM2* EM3*…) is a valid expression. Intensity fac
tors include the ones listed below. The Table 2 below shows

the effort multipliers in the first column while the next columnshowstheeffortestimatedconditionsnamedasverylow,
low, nominal, high, very high, extra high, and productivity
high range:
In COCOMO I, KSLOC’s exponent ranged from 1.05 to
1.2; today, there is only one such value. Concerns like “Have
we constructed this kind of system before?” were modelled
in COCOMO II by decomposing the exponent “b” into a
constant and the sum of five “scaling factors.” Comparable
effort multipliers were introduced in COCOMOII, although
specific parameters were removed, renamed, or added (for
“required level of reuse”, “multiple-site development”, and
“schedule pressure”). All effort multipliers can be broken

and Project categories, along with their respective rating values. We have five products in the dataset, three computers,
five personnel products, and four projects.

**4.3 Features ranking using GA**


The adoption of a meta-heuristic like the genetic algorithm,
which can select features on its own, would make the search
more objective. However, with so many potential permutations in the solution space, it’s fair to question whether
or not an optimal solution is possible when the number of
characteristics is enormous. Genetic algorithms employ an
evolutionary technique to provide optimal solutions. A population should be constructed utilizing subsets of the available
features as a starting point for feature selection. Subsets of
this group are then evaluated using the prediction model. The
criteria used to rank features are displayed in Fig. 5.
Table 4 shows the ranking and scores of each feature using
GA. The ranking and scores of each feature using GA. The
ranking score varies between 0.3 and 0.5 in products, 0.5–0.7
in computers, and 0.1–0.7 in personnel, while in projects, it
varies from 0.3 to 0.75.


**Fig. 5** Feature ranking by GA

GA for each feature. The rankings and total points earned
by each feature according to GA are detailed in Table 5. The

**4.4 Effort estimation**

According to the research presented in the article [9],
the COCOMO II post-architecture technique computes the
amount of work put into developing software (measured in
person months) by utilizing the following equation:

Effort � *A* × *(* SIZE *)E* × *�i* EMi *.* (9)

A multiplicative constant with a value of 2.94 adjusts the
work required for the project based on its unique circumstances. Size is the estimated size of a project expressed
either in unadjusted function points or in kilo source lines
of code. E is an exponential factor that accounts for the relative economies of scale a software project faces as its size

increases. E can also account for the relative diseconomies of

COCOMO II combined the Delphi method and algorithmic cost-estimating methodologies, making it a straightforward and efficient calibration process. It is also an objective
and supportive tool. This model can be replicated and adapted

[6]. However, most of its extensions are still in the experimental stage and need to be correctly calibrated, which is one

of its limitations.


Everything that could be done with the implemented tool
has been done. The uniform crossover technique, tournament
selection mechanism, and mutation rate 0.15 are the GA tuning parameters for optimizing the COCOMO II PA model
coefficients. After several iterations, the optimal solution, as
measured by the fitness function, is found among a group of
candidate solutions. Figure 7 shows the GASVR Features of

COCOMO II Effort Estimation Prediction.

This research presents a GA-SVR technique to estimate
software expenses using the perceptron learning process. The
COCOMO model was used as the basis for this proposal.
According to the findings of recent studies, the GA-SVR
method is one of the most accurate approaches to evaluating the cost of software. Numerous industry professionals
are currently concentrating their efforts on developing GASVR-based software cost estimation methodologies that are
more accurate. Figures 5 and 6 display the estimated work
andtimerequiredtobuildanythingusingthecurrentandoptimized version of COCOMO-II, respectively, and the amount
of work and time needed to develop something. As the results
show, there has been an increase in accuracy in estimating
both the amount of work and the amount of time required.
While the improvement in the work estimation is intangible,
the improvement in the time estimation is significant. It is
also noteworthy that although the estimated amount of effort
for some projects is very different from the actual amount
of effort for those projects, the estimated amount of time
required for development is very accurate. In potential future
research, the reasons for this could be investigated further.

**4.6 Performance of GASVR**

Table 7 shows the comparison of MRE on Models with all
projects. For the first project, the effort was 8.2. GA estimated
23, while SVR MRE was estimated at 17. However, when we
had GASVR, MRE was predicted at 6.
Figure 8 shows the training set MMRE and MDMRE values. At 200 iterations, MMRE was 0.77, and MdMRE was

0.8111, while on the last iteration, 1000, MMRE was 0.55,
and MdMRE was 080. For the testing set (see Fig. 9), MMRE
at 200 iterations was 0.75, while MdMRE was 0.79. At the

end of the 1000 iteration, MMRE was 0.74, and MdMRE

was 0.82.

Figure 10 depicts several PRED values, including 0.5 at

the 800th iteration.

The evaluation process employed every one of the 93
projects in the NASA data set. Table 8 shows the evaluation of
the models. It displays the mean of magnitude relative error
(MRE) of effort estimation and development time estimation

and SCE has a 0.25 PRED value. GA has a 0.5 PRED value,
while our model has a 0.55 PRED value, showing the best

result.

**5 Conclusions**

In developing machine learning models to address diverse
issues confronting businesses and educational institutions,
data scientists are required to surmount several obstacles
related to Model Development in the context of Software
Engineering. Developers working on Machine Learning frequently need to be made aware of how much better off they
would be if they stuck to the processes described in the Software Engineering Development Lifecycle. This is a common
problem. This is because the procedures for constructing
machine learning systems will be distinct from those utilized
by more conventional software systems. This article analyses
these difficulties and practises from a software engineering perspective to better understand how developers could
apply or adapt the standard software engineering approach
to the Machine Learning workflow. In this study, we used
## 123


the COCOMO II Model to forecast a software engineering
model’s effort estimate and effort estimation utilizing a mix
ofmachinelearningapproaches.Thesetechniqueswerecombined with machine learning. Using the COCOMO Model II,
our Genetic Algorithm Support Vector Regressor model has
demonstrated the highest PRED value for effort estimation.
